newsitem.title: USA: GM U.S. sales rise 6.5 percent, Chrysler sales fall.
newsitem.headline: GM U.S. sales rise 6.5 percent, Chrysler sales fall.

text.p: General Motors Corp. Friday posted an unexpected 6.5 percent jump in U.S. sales for July, but the strong numbers were not enough to outshine bigger gains at both Toyota and Honda.
Sales at No. 3 U.S. automaker Chrysler Corp. fell 9.3 percent in July.
GM, the nation's largest automaker, said higher incentive spending on older models drove sales up sharply in the latest month.
GM sold 419,102 cars and trucks in July, up from 393,526 in the same month of 1996. Car sales rose 3 percent to 237,267, while total truck sales shot up 11.5 percent to 181,835.

Analyts had expected GM to post a total decline of about 4 percent. But GM sales surged in the last two weeks of the month, allowing the automaker to report higher sales in every division except Oldsmobile.
GM officials cited a recovery from work stoppages, strong sales of newer models and a change in how it spends incentive money to clear out cars and trucks from the outgoing model year.

The company eliminated the traditional 5 percent discount it gives dealers on every carryover model in late September or early October. In its place, GM began offering July 15 lower finance rates of 2.9 percent or cash rebates ranging from $750 to $1,500 on many of its older cars.
"I think we were just caught off guard a bit in terms of how aggressive our competitors were," said Michael DiGiovanni, who oversees GM's market research and vehicle forecasts.

Reversing June's poor results, GM truck sales were the best ever for a July, with both Chevrolet and GMC setting monthly records. Also up were GM's minivan sales, which company officials said was proof the new Venture, Trans Sport and Silhoutte are catching on with consumers.
Meanwhile, Toyota Motor Corp. and Honda Motor Co. Ltd., continued to outpace the Big Three.
Toyota sales rose 14.6 percent to 108,939. July sales at Honda's American Honda unit soared 31.8 percent to 87,929, an all-time monthly record.
"Hot cars and a hot economy equal record sales," Dick Colliver, Honda division executive vice president, said in a statement.

Sales of the popular Civic jumped 51 percent to 29,995, while Accord sales were up 10.3 percent to 33,865. The Toyota Camry further cemented its lead as the best-selling U.S. car so far this year with an 8.7 percent sales gain in July to 32,555, its best July ever.
At Chrysler, U.S. July vehicle sales fell to 199,662 from 220,139 as the company continued to face tough comparisons with strong year-ago levels.
Overall truck sales for the U.S. No. 3 automaker fell 8 percent to 134,858. Total car sales were 64,804, a decline of 13 percent.

"Some of the totals are lagging a bit behind last year's records, but the market is solid and we're seeing strength in sales of our key products," James Holden, executive vice president of sales and marketing, said in a statement.
Chrysler said minivan sales for the month were 50,547, up 1 percent from last year's 50,156 and a new monthly record.
Ford Motor Co. is scheduled to report sales Aug. 5.
